#9669. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9668. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9667. Comic Panel Detection With a Vision LLM: Pages Into Shots for Under Half a Cent

Founder of Outerframe Studio and creator of ScreenWeaver, an AI workspace for writers and filmmakers.

Founder of Outerframe Studio and creator of ScreenWeaver, an AI workspace for writers and filmmakers.

Founder of Outerframe Studio and creator of ScreenWeaver, an AI workspace for writers and filmmakers.

How ScreenWeaver finds the panels on a comic, webtoon or storyboard page with Gemini Flash, and the small decisions that keep it cheap and safe to run twice.

A comic page is already half a storyboard. Six frames, a reading order, a page number at the bottom. If you want to turn that page into an animated scene, every panel has to become its own image so it can sit on a shot as a reference. Cutting them by hand in an image editor is easy for one page. Do it for a whole chapter and you've spent hours on crop boxes before making a single shot.

Comic panel detection with a vision LLM means sending one page image to a multimodal model, asking it for a bounding box around every panel in reading order, then cutting those boxes on your own server. In ScreenWeaver, where I'm a co-founder, it runs on Gemini Flash and costs between $0.0036 and $0.0048 a page in our measurements.

We shipped it on October 13, 2026. This is a look at how it works, and at the dull decisions around the model call that ended up mattering more than the model itself.

Classic panel detection works, and it's free. The best-known open-source option is Kumiko, the Comics Cutter, which uses OpenCV's contour detection to find panels and can number them left to right or right to left. It runs locally and costs nothing per page.

So why pay for a model call? Because of the pages we actually get:

And we wanted one more thing contours can't give you: a one-line caption per panel, saying who is in it and what happens. That caption travels with the cropped image, so the agent that builds the shots later doesn't have to look at every panel again to know what it is.

A contour finder sees rectangles. A notebook page full of handwriting has plenty of rectangles that aren't panels.

To be fair to Kumiko: if your pages are clean, with clear gutters around every frame, it's free, offline and worth trying first.

Kumiko, the open-source comics cutter, on GitHub. Screenshot: github.com/njean42/kumiko, October 2026.

One page per call. The page is turned upright, flattened on white, shrunk so its longest side is 1,568 pixels and sent as a JPEG. The system prompt is short. It asks for every panel in reading order, each with a box and a caption of 80 characters at most, and then it spends most of its words on what to leave out: the gutters, page numbers, titles, and notes written beside or below a frame on a storyboard sheet. A speech balloon inside a frame stays part of the panel.

Two edge cases are spelled out because they come up constantly. If the whole page is one picture, the model returns one box around it. If the page has no picture at all (a text page, a blank page), it returns nothing.

The box format comes straight from Google. Gemini is trained to return boxes as [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] on a 0 to 1000 scale relative to the image, and the Gemini API documentation tells you to scale those values back to your original image size yourself. We use structured output, so the response is a JSON object we validate with a schema rather than text we parse with regular expressions. Reasoning is switched off for this call: it's a perception task, and thinking tokens would only add cost.

The object detection section of Google's Gemini API docs, where the 0 to 1000 box scale is defined. Screenshot: ai.google.dev, October 2026.

You don't trust it as is. Model output is input from outside your code, and one malformed box is enough to break a crop. Before anything gets cut, every box goes through the same small filter:

Then the server cuts each box out of the full-resolution page (the model only saw the 1,568 px version, but the coordinates are fractions, so they apply to the original) and stores every panel as its own image, labelled "Page N, panel K" with its caption.

None of this is clever. The filter is about twenty lines of plain code, and it's the reason a bad box costs you one missing panel instead of a failed import.

Where the model call sits in ScreenWeaver's panel detection. Diagram: ScreenWeaver.

The measured cost sits between $0.0036 and $0.0048 a page. One real run: a 20-page storyboard with six panels a page came to $0.097 in total. For budgeting, the app counts about $0.005 a page, which is one credit.

Because this is the step of an import that spends money, it has guard rails:

The model call is the cheap part. The expensive part is running it twice by accident.

This is the decision I'd copy into any pipeline that calls a paid model on files.

The panels are saved on the page record itself. If an import is retried, after a timeout or because the agent decided to add more crops, the stored panels are reused. The model isn't called again, nobody pays again, and the boxes don't move. That last part matters more than the money: if a second run nudged every box by a few pixels, every shot that already uses a panel would quietly change.

The IDs make this work. A page's ID is built from a hash of the file plus the page number, and a crop's ID from the page ID plus a hash of the box. Import the same PDF next week and the server recognizes every page and every panel it already rendered, and renders nothing twice.

Failures stay local too. If the model call fails on page 14, that page is reported as panelsFailed and the import carries on with page 15. You get panels for every other page and a clear note about the one that needs another try, instead of an error and nothing.

What a first import costs and what a re-import costs. Figures from ScreenWeaver's own measurements, October 2026.

Webtoons, yes, with one preparation step. A webtoon episode is often a single strip thousands of pixels tall. Shrunk to 1,568 px on its longest side, the panels would be too small to box. So a long strip goes in as a series of images about the height of a page. We did this on Imaginarium, a webtoon adapted into an animated series in ScreenWeaver: pages of episode 1 went in, the panels came out, and each one became the reference for an animated shot.

Manga, with a caveat I'd rather say out loud. The prompt asks for "reading order" and doesn't say which direction. We haven't measured the result on a run of right-to-left pages yet, so I won't claim the order comes out right every time. If you're processing manga in volume today, check the order on a few pages first. This is one place where Kumiko's explicit right-to-left switch is simply better.

Storyboard sheets are where the vision model earns its money. On that notebook page of six pencil sketches, the notes under each frame ("plan large", "travelling avant", "insert fleur") stay out of the cropped images. The agent read them separately and used them to set the framing and camera move of shots S14 to S19, with each sketch attached to its shot.

A real notebook page imported through the ScreenWeaver MCP, each sketch stored as its own image. Diagram: ScreenWeaver.

Panels on their own are just images. The rest of the chain is what turns a page into a scene:

Then a person opens the Storyboard and Production tabs and launches the generations. The MCP server prepares; it never generates images or video on its own. That boundary is deliberate: the agent does the tedious part, the author keeps the button that spends real money on footage.

If you want to see it on a real webtoon, the Imaginarium pages and the shots they became are on our webtoon page.

Which model does ScreenWeaver use for panel detection?

Gemini Flash (google/gemini-3.8-flash) through an AI gateway, with structured output and reasoning switched off.

Can I detect comic panels without paying for an API?

Yes. Kumiko does it locally with OpenCV contour detection. It suits clean pages with clear gutters best.

Up to 40, in reading order. Boxes under 1% of the page are dropped.

Detection keeps balloons inside the panel. They're left out later, when the panel is used as a reference for a shot.

If you're building something similar, spend your time on the code after the model call, and store what the model told you so you never pay for the same page twice. The panel boxes were the easy part.

MCP Server Best Practices: Our AI Agent Retyped 22 of 127 Scenes and Called It Done

Founder of Outerframe Studio and creator of ScreenWeaver, an AI workspace for writers and filmmakers.

#9665. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

#9664. I Vibe-Coded a Layer-1 Blockchain to Give Everyone Free AI

Builder of AIcuNet, an open-source Layer-1 blockchain. Vibe-coding in public, with several AI models as reviewers.

Builder of AIcuNet, an open-source Layer-1 blockchain. Vibe-coding in public, with several AI models as reviewers.

Builder of AIcuNet, an open-source Layer-1 blockchain. Vibe-coding in public, with several AI models as reviewers.

An honest builder's story: one developer, a lot of AI assistance, a legal MIT-licensed base, adversarial review by several different AI models — and a live network that mines on an ordinary laptop.

Most useful AI today lives behind a login you don't control. It is rented, rate-limited, and one policy change away from changing the rules on you. The tools that could decentralize it — blockchains — mostly went the other way: heavier, ASIC-dominated, treating compute as wasted heat instead of useful work.

So I asked a stubborn question: what if a blockchain could run on almost any PC, and the same network that secures it could also serve AI to everyone on it — for free?

Not "free" as a marketing word. Free as in: you lend the network a slice of your machine — CPU and RAM today, storage and GPU on the roadmap — and in return you get access to a shared pool of intelligence. Support the network, get the AI. That is the whole deal, and whatever is still on the roadmap is named as such below.

I called it AIcuNet. And I will be upfront about how it got built, because that is half the story.

I am one developer. I did not hand-write a consensus engine from scratch in a cave. I vibe-coded this — building with heavy AI assistance, iterating in natural language, letting agents draft, refactor and test while I steered the architecture and made the calls.

First, I started from a real, legal base. AIcuNet builds on an existing open-source Layer-1 released under the MIT License — the attribution is spelled out in the License section at the end of this article and in the repository's LICENSE and NOTICE. I did not pretend to invent time-driven proof-of-work. I stood on a working L1 and built the parts I actually cared about on top.

Second, "AI wrote it" is not a free pass — so I stress-tested it as if it weren't. The codebase went through a multi-pass security review by several different AI models, each with a different method — static call-graph analysis, a runtime harness, fresh independent reads — cross-checked against each other, followed by a round of hardening fixes. I am not publishing the findings, and I am not calling this an independent certification: no outside firm has signed off on the code. What I will say is the lesson: the value isn't the number of reviewers, it's the diversity of method. Three passes with the same technique find the same bug. Three orthogonal methods find three different classes of bug — including the quiet, irreversible ones that never throw an error.

Vibe-coding got me to a working L1 fast. Adversarial review is what makes me willing to put it in public.

I am going to be precise about stage, because "coming soon" is how trust dies.

Phase 1 — the L1 consensus — is live. One public chain since 12 July 2026, with mining and a web wallet. Time is sliced into 3-second slots; one slot, one block, one chain. On paper the protocol handles up to 1,000 transactions per second (up to 3,000 transactions per 3-second block) — one of the higher figures among decentralized PoW networks. That is the design ceiling, not a measurement: a public benchmark on a test network is next on the list, and I expect the real number to land above the theory. A transfer is considered final after a handful of blocks — about half a minute.

Today the launch-phase nodes that carry the network run in four countries on three continents. As of publishing, the chain stands at over 2.5 million blocks — you can check it live here: https://aicunet.com/en/mining-map/#status. A node synced from zero on 1 October 2026 matched the network at block #2,000,000 — the boring, beautiful property you want from a blockchain.

The network is built in layers: consensus first, then a resource layer, then GPU and AI compute. Phase 2 (a resource layer where nodes contribute storage and light compute) and Phase 3 (GPU and AI compute on the network's own resources) are concepts on the roadmap — not shipped. Beyond them lies network expansion — a horizon, not a plan with dates. The dApp layer sits on top of Phase 1, and it has its own section below. I am not going to show you a mockup and call it a product; what is done and what comes next is listed on the roadmap.

It is an early-stage, working network, small on purpose, and the code is open under MIT at https://github.com/aicunet/aicunet-core.

Here is the part that has moved since I first wrote this story. The smart-contract engine is already in the network's code, and contracts have been enabled since the first block. Contracts are written in JavaScript, the most widely used programming language, so there is no new language to learn. The engine comes with a development environment for dApps — the DApp IDE: projects, templates and a test run before anything touches the chain. An app's interface can live in the chain itself, next to its logic, and users can issue their own tokens.

Because the network has no fees, nobody has to buy "gas" before pressing a button in an app. That is the part of Web3 I actually care about: an app that belongs to the people who use it, with no toll booth at the entrance.

The network's first application, Miner's Hour, has been running on the network since 30 September 2026 in a trial period: once an hour, a bonus goes to one participant picked at random among the miners, and every miner has the same chance, however much hardware they bring. Equal odds are deliberate: mining already rewards power, and a bonus weighted by power would simply pay the biggest machine twice. The contract keeps the list of miners itself; the project cannot add or remove a participant, and the list is visible in the contract's data. The bonus pool is funded by the project.

Opening the engine to developers is the next step. Until you can build on it yourself, I am not going to call dApps live.

A network upgrade is planned that gives smart contracts data storage and cryptographic functions. On a live chain, an upgrade is the riskiest moment there is — if nodes disagree about the new rules, the chain splits. So the upgrade ran on a test network first, built from a copy of the live network's code. Two things had to hold, and both did: the chain did not split when the nodes crossed the upgrade point, and a contract created before the upgrade kept working after it.

What that test does not prove yet is how the switch behaves in a larger network with outside nodes, and I would rather say so than pretend a small test covers everything. There is no date for the upgrade in this article on purpose: it goes on the roadmap as done when it is done.

A few decisions that make AIcuNet what it is:

The token stack is three simple layers: Axinit (AXNT) rewards the nodes, CuJoule measures compute, and AI Commons is meant to make the resulting intelligence accessible. One line: AIcuNet turns distributed compute into public intelligence.

Here is where it gets a little unusual. AIcuNet's economics borrow a 19th-century idea: an economist of that time described money as an elastic measure of trust and labor, rather than a rigid, artificially scarce asset.

A hard supply cap is the opposite philosophy. The argument of a 19th-century economic-philosophical treatise was that money should stretch and contract with the real economy. AIcuNet takes that idea and ties it to work that is proven cryptographically — first mining, later proof-of-resource — not to somebody's word. The full story belongs in the tokenomics article; here is what is already true:

This is not a promise — it is how the accounts are set up. And to be explicit: AXNT is not an investment asset, and nothing on this page is a claim about price or returns.

Because I don't think the answer to concentrated AI is more concentration — I think it is networks nobody owns. The missing piece is a network that turns the PC you already own into a share of a public, AI-serving commons — open, hard to switch off, and with the same rules for everyone from the first block.

I also think the honest version of the "AI built this" story matters. This is an experiment: can a solo developer, vibe-coding and backing it with real adversarial review, ship infrastructure that is actually good for people? I would rather find out in public.

So here is an open invitation: request an invite at aicunet.com — the Windows node package goes to invited participants first — and run a node on a laptop. Read the consensus. Try the wallet. A public bug-bounty program is planned.

Two things come next, and I will publish both: a transaction-throughput benchmark on a test network, and the tokenomics — how the block reward is tied to the growth of the network. If this story gets any interest, that is where it continues.

The goal underneath all of it is embarrassingly simple: put the benefits of AI into people's hands, for free. If that is the future you want too, this is the network to build together.

AIcuNet is based on the Tera blockchain software by the Tera Core developers (Yuriy Ivanov, progr76@gmail.com):https://github.com/terablockchain/teraBase commit: 8d65eb4a6ef5eb98ca1aea61ae73f805b681dc92 (release 2651, 2022-05-24).The LICENSE file of the base commit is the MIT License (with the author's "Not for evil" note); AIcuNet uses the code under that license.

AIcuNet is an independent project and is not affiliated with, sponsored or endorsed by the Tera Foundation, EMPERA NETWORK or the upstream author.

AIcuNet is a Layer-1 blockchain under the MIT License (attribution above). Phase-1 consensus is live since 12 July 2026; the dApp engine is in the code and its first app, Miner's Hour, runs in a trial period; the resource and AI layers are on the roadmap. Built with AI assistance, hardened by multi-pass review. Site: https://aicunet.com · Roadmap: https://aicunet.com/en/roadmap/ · Code: https://github.com/aicunet/aicunet-core · Live chain: https://aicunet.com/en/mining-map/#status.

#9662. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9661. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

#9660. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9659. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9658. Why JWT Signature Verification Alone Can't Prevent Token Replay

Cybersecurity architect with 17+ years of experience in IAM, GRC, SAP security, Zero Trust, cloud security, and AI security.

Cybersecurity architect with 17+ years of experience in IAM, GRC, SAP security, Zero Trust, cloud security, and AI security.

Cybersecurity architect with 17+ years of experience in IAM, GRC, SAP security, Zero Trust, cloud security, and AI security.

Why signature verification alone cannot prevent cross-API token replay.

For API developers and security architects building resource servers behind a shared identity provider.

An access token can be correctly signed, issued by a trusted authorization server, and still unexpired, yet be the wrong credential for the API receiving it. When several APIs trust the same issuer, a resource server that verifies the signature but skips the audience check may accept a token that was minted for a completely different service. Nothing looks broken: authentication succeeds, standard authentication logs may show no obvious failure, and the trust boundary between APIs has already failed.

This is not a weakness in OAuth itself. It is a failure to enforce the boundary that OAuth token validation is designed to provide. The scenario below is hypothetical, uses fictional hostnames, and is built from publicly documented specifications. It illustrates a configuration weakness, not a confirmed vulnerability in any specific product.

Many OAuth 2.0 deployments issue access tokens as JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), which lets resource servers validate them locally. A JWT has a header, a payload, and a signature. The payload carries claims such as these:

The timestamps in these examples are illustrative. Any real test should generate tokens with valid issuance and expiration times.

The aud claim is how a resource server decides whether a token was meant for it. The token above is intended for the Inventory API. It should not authorize requests to a Finance API simply because both APIs trust the same identity provider.

A valid token is not necessarily a valid token for your API.

Centralized identity is operationally convenient. One authorization server may serve dozens or hundreds of APIs, and those APIs often share validation libraries, issuer configuration, and public signing keys.

The risk appears when teams treat a successful signature check as proof that a request is authorized.

Consider two hypothetical services that trust https://identity.example.com:

An employee legitimately obtains a token for the Inventory API.

If the Finance API validates signature, issuer, and expiry but never checks the audience, it may accept that Inventory token.

Whether this leads to unauthorized data access depends on the Finance API's remaining authorization checks, but the first boundary has already failed: the API accepted a credential that was never issued for it.

A client requests access to the Inventory API, and the authorization server returns a token signed with its private key:

It checks that the signature is valid, the issuer is trusted, and the token has not expired.

However, it never asks whether the token was issued for the Finance API.

If its authorization logic then treats the token's claims as sufficient for the requested operation, the request succeeds.

This is a cross-resource token replay weakness.

The authorization server did not issue this token for the Finance API.

The Finance API interpreted a token meant for another resource as acceptable authorization evidence on its own.

What it should have returned is a rejection along these lines, using the invalid_token error code defined in RFC 6750:

The error_description text is illustrative. RFC 6750 does not prescribe this wording, and the exact message varies by implementation.

A digital signature answers one question:

Was this token signed by a trusted authority, and is its content unchanged?

Audience validation answers a different question:

Was this token intended for this resource server?

A token can pass the first check and fail the second.

Cryptographic validity and authorization validity must be evaluated separately.

When a token lists multiple audiences, it may be accepted by more than one resource server. This broadens the potential impact if the token is disclosed, although each API must still independently enforce scopes and authorization policies.

RFC 9700 recommends restricting a token to a single resource server where feasible, or otherwise to a small set.

Several OAuth and JWT specifications address this security boundary.

RFC 8707 allows a client to identify the protected resource it wants to access.

The authorization server can use this information to issue an audience-restricted token for that resource.

RFC 9068 requires resource servers using that profile to validate that the aud claim contains an identifier the resource server expects for itself.

A token that does not contain an acceptable audience must be rejected.

The specification also defines the at+jwt token type to help distinguish access tokens from other JWTs.

RFC 9700 recommends audience-restricting access tokens to reduce the risk of a stolen or leaked token being replayed against an unintended resource server.

The principle across these specifications is consistent:

A resource server must not accept an access token only because it trusts the issuer. It must also confirm that the token was intended for it.

Consider a simplified Python implementation using PyJWT.

The following function verifies the signature and issuer but deliberately disables audience validation:

This does not mean that applications using PyJWT are inherently vulnerable.

The weakness is the decision to disable audience validation without enforcing an equivalent resource-binding control.

The following version explicitly defines the expected audience and checks that the JWT is typed as an access token.

This is an illustration of audience enforcement, not a complete RFC 9068 validator. That profile also requires claims such as sub, iat, jti, and client_id, along with other profile-specific checks.

A token issued only for the Inventory API now fails when presented to the Finance API.

The typ check applies to JWT access tokens following RFC 9068. Other token formats require validation appropriate to their documented token profile.

Do not relax token-type checks merely to make an otherwise incompatible token pass validation.

In production, the verification key must also come from a trusted, securely configured source, and the API must enforce scopes and endpoint-level authorization.

Audience validation is essential, but it does not replace those checks.

Normal workflows may continue working when audience validation is missing.

Legitimate users receive legitimate tokens, APIs respond, and authentication dashboards show expected activity.

Monitoring that focuses only on signature and issuer validation may not distinguish a token presented to its intended API from one presented to a different API and accepted by mistake.

Both requests involve authentic tokens from the same trusted issuer.

The absence of signature failures can create a false sense of security.

Monitoring should therefore ask not only whether a token is valid, but whether it is valid for the resource receiving it.

The following tests belong in authorized development or staging environments.

These are expected outcomes for a correctly configured API, not findings from a real system. Observed results should only be published after the tests have actually been executed.

Accepted, subject to scopes and authorization policy

Missing aud where the profile requires it

Audience validation and scope enforcement solve different problems.

An API that checks audience but ignores permissions can still expose sensitive operations.

Secure API authorization requires multiple controls working together.

Each resource server should maintain an explicit list of acceptable audience identifiers.

Tokens intended for unrelated services should be rejected.

Trusted issuers must be explicitly configured.

Do not derive issuer trust from untrusted token content.

Use trusted verification keys and an explicit allow-list of signing algorithms.

Never let a token select an arbitrary verification key or disable signature verification.

Validate exp and other applicable time-based claims.

Short-lived access tokens reduce the potential exposure period when bearer tokens leak, although they do not correct missing audience checks.

A token intended for an API should authorize only the operations that its subject or client is permitted to perform.

Resource servers must enforce permissions at the endpoint and object levels.

An OpenID Connect ID token is intended to convey authentication information to the client.

It should not be accepted as an API access token merely because its signature is valid.

Explicit access-token typing, such as at+jwt, helps distinguish token purposes.

Audience restrictions limit where an access token can be used.

Sender-constrained mechanisms, such as mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP, RFC 9449), can additionally restrict who can successfully present it.

These controls address different aspects of token replay and provide stronger protection when combined.

Security telemetry should capture audience-validation failures and other token rejection reasons without logging raw bearer tokens.

Repeated wrong-audience requests may indicate integration mistakes, misconfiguration, or attempts to cross API trust boundaries.

Zero Trust emphasizes continuous verification and limiting implicit trust.

An API that accepts any token from a trusted issuer reintroduces the kind of implicit trust that Zero Trust architectures are intended to reduce.

A centralized identity provider provides a common trust foundation, but every resource server still needs to enforce its own authorization boundary.

The same principle applies to service-to-service communication, microservices, cloud-native workloads, and machine identities.

As organizations expand their APIs and automated integrations, resource-specific token validation becomes increasingly important.

The question should not simply be whether a request carries a valid token.

It should be whether that token is valid for this resource, this operation, and this security context.

Treat audience validation as a mandatory security control, not a library default that developers assume is enabled.

Make it part of API security reviews and test it explicitly, just as authentication itself is tested.

A valid digital signature proves that a token is authentic and has not been modified.

It does not prove that the token was issued for every API that trusts the same authorization server.

The solution is not to abandon centralized identity or JWT-based access tokens.

It is to validate tokens completely: issuer, signature, expiration, token type, audience, and the permissions required by the requested operation.

Never confuse trust in an issuer with trust in every token that issuer creates.

A secure API verifies who issued a token, which resource it was issued for, and what it permits.

Note: All hostnames, identifiers, and scenarios in this article are fictional illustrations based on publicly available specifications.

Cybersecurity architect with 17+ years of experience in IAM, GRC, SAP security, Zero Trust, cloud security, and AI security.
