#9656. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9655. How to get a transcript of a TikTok or Instagram Reel (3 ways)

Short videos are where a lot of ideas live now, but TikTok and Instagram don't give you a "copy transcript" button. Here are three ways to get the words out of a Reel or a TikTok, from zero setup to fully local.

Many TikToks and Reels show auto-generated captions. They're fine for reading along, but you can't copy or download them, and they only exist if the creator turned them on.

Web tools fetch the video for you and return text in a few seconds. I built one, TranscribeLink: paste a public TikTok, Instagram Reel, YouTube or X link and you get a word-for-word transcript with punctuation, in the language that was spoken. It can label speakers, translate into 50+ languages and export TXT, DOCX, PDF or SRT. The first 20 minutes are free without an account. Other tools exist too; pick whichever fits your volume and budget.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of TranscribeLink.

#9654. Pocket shut down. Its export is five CSV columns, and this is how I import them

Pocket closed on July 8, 2025, and its exports could be downloaded until October 8, 2025. If you got yours, you have a CSV file, and that file is what is left of everything you saved there.

I built KeepFinding, a read-later app, and its import reads that file as it is. Here is what is actually in the Pocket export and the Raindrop.io one, and what my importer does with each column.

Pocket's download may be a .zip. The data is the .csv inside, and if there are several, you import them one after another. Each has five columns:

That is all of it. No images and no excerpts, so those are fetched later.

Raindrop's CSV has eleven columns: id,title,note,excerpt,url,folder,tags,created,cover,highlights,favorite. What matters for a parser:

I keep the title, note, excerpt (as the description), folder, tags, date and favorite. I do not read id or cover, and highlights do not come across.

People rename files, so the format is read from the first line. A Pocket header has url and time_added plus status or tags. A Raindrop header has url, one of excerpt, cover or highlights, and folder or created. Any other CSV with a URL column takes a generic path. One test feeds the Pocket fixture in as export.txt and expects Pocket back.

The CSV reader is about 35 lines with no dependency: quoted line breaks, "" as an escaped quote, a byte order mark ignored, and the delimiter sniffed from the header.

Pocket writes seconds, Raindrop writes ISO strings, and some files write milliseconds. Instead of a branch per source, the parser guesses the unit from the size of the number and refuses anything implausible:

A date before 1995 or more than a day in the future is dropped, not guessed. The link still imports without it.

In KeepFinding a list is a prompt you write, like "podcasts under 20 minutes", and a rule answers the simple ones. Each Pocket tag becomes a topic on the link, and a list with the prompt tagged recipes gathers everything you tagged recipes.

For Raindrop, each top-level collection in a backup can become a list the same way: the import writes a tagged prompt and names the list after the collection. Nested collection names become topics.

Real data found a bug here. I ran two Raindrop exports published on GitHub through the real import path. In one, 28 of the 96 rows sat in Unsorted, which is Raindrop's inbox and not a subject, and the import turned it into a topic and a list. The fix strips it from the path:

Every URL is normalised first: utm_*, fbclid and other tracking parameters go, www. and trailing slashes go, http becomes https. So example.com/hello-world?utm_source=pocket and example.com/hello-world are one link, and that pair is in my Pocket test fixture.

Inside the file, the first occurrence wins. Against your library, links you already have are skipped. My first summary called both "already saved", which was wrong on a first import, so the dry run now returns repeated for the file and duplicates for the library. Importing the same file twice adds nothing.

Fetching every page while importing would mean thousands of page loads, so the import writes rows from the file alone, 100 links per request, and marks each row as owed a fetch. A second endpoint fills in covers and summaries ten rows at a time. Every batch is checked against the library again, so a reload halfway through leaves a consistent library. A page that is gone keeps its title and link.

Limits: 5 MB and 5,000 links per file, 3,000 links per account. Archived links count, because leaving them out let one Pocket file full of archived rows walk past the cap.

When I first wrote this, Instapaper's CSV only came in through the generic path, and its Archive and Starred folders became topics instead of archiving or starring. That was not correct enough to promise, so each of these now has its own parser:

Detection works the same way: an Instapaper header has url, selection, folder and timestamp, and a Reader header has url, title, document_tags, saved_date and location.

You do not need an account. Open keepfind.ing/pocket, keepfind.ing/raindrop or keepfind.ing/instapaper, save any link on Home, and KeepFinding starts a trial library in your browser. Settings then shows Your data, where you choose your export file, and it tells you what it found before anything is added. A trial library takes up to 80 links, and it comes with you if you create an account later.

A question for anyone who still has one of these files: does your header match the ones above? My fixtures are trimmed copies of the exports I could find, and if yours has a column or quirk I have not seen, I would rather fix the parser than guess.

#9653. Star Wars and the Revenge of Midterms

The big and beautiful Blue Wave did its thing, as expected. Texas is (not) to be neglected. Should Trump pack his bags? Not necessarily, but he should reflect on his legacy like never before. What could it be? I can think of one word in particular.

Thanks to Trump, we can freely use the R-word. Talking about Texas, is there anyone else who’s been more enthusiastic about it than Joe Rogan? Free at last, free at last, thank Trump, Joe Rogan is free to say retards, at last. I’m paraphrasing, but not exaggerating. Feel free to fact-check me. I can ask ChatGPT to find me episodes where Rogan considers the liberation of retardation as one of the “great culture victories.” I can, but I won’t.

“The Brady Bunch” star Maureen McCormick, who’s also a Special Olympics ambassador, said that Joe Rogan celebrating the resurgence of the r-word “ignores the terrible hurt” the slur causes people with disabilities. “This is not a victory,” she wrote on X, prompting more than 8,000 replies from supporters and detractors alike. “It is a regression.”

Joe isn’t the only one. Asmongold also likes to use and defend that word a lot. This one I won’t paraphrase. I have to be precise:

"I would much rather pay for rockets to go to the moon than pay to keep a bunch of Africans from starving. It's not my obligation to keep every African alive. I don't care about that."

If that’s not a retarted thing to think or say or both, I don’t know what is. You can’t choose to deal with a mental disability, but you can choose not to be a racist. My heart goes out to our favorite rocketman:

“Elon Musk used the word in response to a Finnish researcher who called Musk the “largest spreader of disinformation in human history.” Use of the slur more than doubled on X, the platform Musk owns, in the two days after he made that January post, researchers from Montclair State University found. More than 312,000 subsequent posts made on X in that span contained the r-word, wrote co-author Bond Benton, a professor of communication at the New Jersey university.”

James Sexton, who’s the world’s most famous divorce lawyer, had one of his many brilliant takes on Gen Zs. I’m paraphrasing. They (Gen Z) like to give new names to old things that already exist. Aura for charisma, and so on. They’re rediscovering and renaming the world. It was about time for Hayden Christensen to be rehabilitated.

Anakin Skywalker couldn’t save MAGA in the midterms, but there’s always A New Hope for Trump’s third term.

What are we doing? Where are we going? If you stay too long and dig too deep into the manosphere, one day you may realize that Sharia Law is the logical outcome.

When I was a kid, I wanted to be a Jedi. I also wanted to write my version of an open letter to Arthur C. Clarke. I had an idea of sending him a cradle toy with a small monolith instead of a baby. In my letter, I’d explain that we shouldn’t go to the stars unless we explore our home planet first. Exploring and fixing. Unlike Asmongold, I think we have more pressing old matters than building new rockets.

Star Wars Gen Z edition is tempting. I understand. George Carlin had something else in mind when he said: “It's a big club and you ain't in it.” Fascism is a small club, and you better not be in it. I respect the visual appeal of the Empire’s Hugo Boss vibe, but as a Slav and subhuman (Untermensch) according to Nazi racial ideology, I have to accept diversity and inclusion of the Rebels as a lesser evil. My grandfather took part in liberating a concentration camp in my hometown without second thoughts. He knew that after Jews and Roma, there would be more room for other subhumans.

Anakin memes are all fun and games until you realize the scope of extremist problems. Anakin and younglings. Order 66. Build rockets. F… retards and Africans.

Can you imagine what’s going to happen when Gen Z rediscovers Battlestar Galactica? Trans Cylon vibes and our tribes.

Lindsay Clancy and the AI Children of the Corn

#9652. 51 Thanksgiving dessert recipes for a sweet holiday: From cookies to cake — and of course, plenty of pie.

Of course, we had to start with pumpkin pie. This is a rich, well-spiced pie, thanks to a powerful punch of ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper. Two hints for a better result: Mix the filling a day in advance to give the spices a chance to bloom, and be sure to remove the pie from the oven while the center is still wobbly, as overcooking it will cause the filling to crack.

Want even more spice in your pumpkin pie? This spice-forward recipe is for you. Using powerful Vietnamese cinnamon — with its more robust flavor profile — gives the pie an even spicier kick. Meanwhile, the filling is super silky-smooth thanks to a few tablespoons of corn syrup mixed in.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

With its retro vibe, this play on classic chiffon pie is noteworthy for its tender rye crust and its bright, light chiffon filling. The zesty cranberry curd and smooth, sweet Swiss meringue play beautifully together. And the gelatin helps the filling set just right so that once refrigerated, the pie can be sliced neatly. Tart and airy, this pie is an excellent counterpoint to a heavy feast.

Shop the recipe: Organic Medium Rye Flour

Intimidated by pie? Don't be! Our guide on How to Bake Pie has everything you need for a successful, stress-free bake.

This double-crusted beauty is generously filled with sweet-tart apples and spiced with cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice. But the real secret to its flavorful filling is boiled cider, one of our favorite fall ingredients. The sticky tart-sweet syrup adds an extra depth of apple flavor to make this classic pie stand out from the crowd.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Boiled Cider and Instant ClearJel

This unusual method for baking apple pie caught our eye years ago, when a reader sent it via e-mail. But it’s not just a stunt: Baking a pie in a paper grocery bag gives you a beautifully golden brown, perfectly cooked pie, with toothsome yet tender apples (which soften better thanks to the steam trapped by the bag) beneath a streusel topping.

This beloved pie is made much like pumpkin pie, but with mashed sweet potatoes for nuanced flavor and heavy cream for an especially rich custard. Top it with toasted molasses meringue (if you want the pie to be reminiscent of the classic yams and marshmallow dish served at Thanksgiving), or for a simpler option, with freshly whipped cream. (And for a more unconventional version, try this striking Purple Sweet Potato Pie.)

This traditional pie doesn’t use corn syrup — instead, it’s sweetened entirely with brown sugar. The filling is silky smooth, and the pecans on top toast nicely as the pie bakes. Be sure to use high-quality vanilla extract for well-rounded flavor; an optional handful of chopped bittersweet chocolate is a nice addition, too.

If you’re intimidated by pie (or just don’t have time to chill and roll out pie dough) this easier version of pecan pie is for you. A buttery, brown-sugar shortbread crust cradles a gooey honey-sweetened pecan filling. These bars keep well for days, so they’re perfect for baking ahead of Thanksgiving.

This recipe takes classic pecan pie a step further by adding chocolate chips to the filling. The chocolate beautifully complements the pecans' nuttiness; if you choose bittersweet chocolate, it cuts the pie's overall sweetness, allowing all of the flavors to shine more brightly.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Bittersweet Chocolate Chips

Baker's tip: Make and freeze your pie crust early to get ahead on pie prep.

This creamy, decadent pie is positively bursting with maple flavor — be sure to use the best maple syrup you can find and a dash of natural maple flavor to enhance it. One bite of the brûléed maple sugar top and the silky-smooth filling will have you reconsidering your regular rotation of cream pies this Thanksgiving.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar. If you’re only in charge of dessert this year and want to flex a little, this recipe is an impressive (and tasty!) way to do so.

Shop the recipe: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

Mash-up pies are an easy way to please your guests without making multiple pies. This recipe has the best of both worlds: a smooth layer of spiced pumpkin custard plus a rich pecan topping. It’s best made a day ahead so that the flavors can settle, plus there’s one less dish to worry about on Thanksgiving Day.

Shop the recipe: Adjustable Pie Crust Shield

Is there anything cuter than a mini Thanksgiving pie? Filled with a pre-cooked, perfectly spiced filling that’s enhanced with tart boiled cider, these bite-sized treats can be topped with a woven lattice or streusel.

This tart-sweet cake is easy to throw together — made with melted butter, the one-bowl batter is mixed by hand then poured directly over sugared cranberries. If you have cranberries leftover from making sauce or just want to highlight these seasonal berries in other ways, make this cake.

Shop the recipe: Pure Almond Extract and Sparkling Sugar

This stunning pumpkin swirl cake is more than just good looks: It also has a soft, plush texture, thanks to cake flour and sour cream, and a deep pumpkin flavor paired with fragrant vanilla. It starts with one base batter that gets flavored two ways, creating two distinct colors for a striking visual contrast when sliced.

For a more traditional dessert, try this pumpkin-y layer cake. It’s moist and slightly dense from the pumpkin purée, with a tangy cream cheese frosting and sticky caramel glaze.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

In this unabashedly apple-forward apple cake, there are so many apple slices and so little batter, you’ll wonder how (and if) it will hold together. But never fear: As the batter rises in the oven, it knits those slices together to create a tender cake that’s almost creamy and custardy due to the abundance of fruit.

Shop the recipe: Almond Flour and Pure Almond Extract

The pumpkin and pumpkin-friendly spices (cloves, cinnamon, allspice) in this cake meld surprisingly well with the chocolate chips studded throughout. This dark, moist Bundt cake is rich enough to serve unfrosted, and it's just the ticket when you want to serve a dessert that's substantial, yet not too sweet, to finish your Thanksgiving meal. And it keeps well for days, so you can bake it early in the week to help prep ahead.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

This golden cake is rich, moist, and subtly spiced to complement, rather than overshadow, the natural flavor of sweet potatoes. It also includes a crunchy pecan crust on both the top and bottom, along with a touch of maple syrup in the cake for sweetness. Get the recipe: Pecan-Crusted Sweet Potato Pound Cake

With a hidden swirl of coffee-flavored filling, this stunning cake adds an extra dimension to your holiday table. It’s like a pumpkin spice latte in dessert form — and also secretly whole wheat!

Wondering how far ahead you can make your cake? Here's how long cake lasts in the fridge and at room temp.

This cake is an old favorite of our readers, with over 300 five-star reviews. It's a recipe where the whole is definitely more than the sum of the parts: The moist, semi-chunky cake is packed with four cups of apples, then spread with the frosting equivalent of brown sugar fudge. The whole thing comes together by hand in one bowl, so it also fits easily into your Thanksgiving prep.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

Why decide between cheesecake and pie when you can have both? This eye-catching two-toned recipe pairs custardy pumpkin pie with creamy cheesecake for a dessert that will satisfy everyone.

For an all-pumpkin Thanksgiving cheesecake, there’s this classic version, which transforms pumpkin pie into a silky, velvety filling. Because it needs to chill before serving, this cheesecake is an excellent candidate for baking a day ahead of Thanksgiving.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cheesecake with Gingersnap Crust

Shop the recipe: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

We did the testing: This is the best way to keep your cheesecake from cracking.

It’s right there in the name: This is an easy, failproof cheesecake that comes together quickly and bakes up beautifully. You don’t even need a water bath! Top with maple- or bourbon-spiked whipped cream to dress it up for the holiday; details are in the recipe tips at the bottom of our Homemade Whipped Cream recipe.

For a fall-forward cheesecake, turn to this seasonal recipe. The texture of the filling is ultra-smooth and creamy, and the maple flavor is apparent, yet subtle — the secret is natural maple flavor paired with maple syrup. The pecan crust, meanwhile, is a nutty, salty counterbalance to the filling.

Shop the recipe: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

If you’re looking for a celebratory yet unexpected dessert for your table, we recommend this recipe. A heavy pour of Irish whiskey cream liqueur (save some for your after-dinner coffee!) flavors the smooth, light filling, while silky chocolate ganache adorns the top. Oven space at a premium while you prep Thanksgiving dinner? This dessert is no-bake, so you can save some room in the cooking schedule.

With its burnished top and custardy interior, this cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This flourless cake is incredibly rich — like sliceable fudge sauce. A thick icing of chocolate ganache glaze takes it over the top, but if you want something a touch lighter after a heavy Thanksgiving feast, top it instead with a dusting of confectioners’ sugar and a spoonful of barely sweetened whipped cream.

Baker's tip: Make your whipped cream in a Mason jar, especially helpful if you're bringing dessert to someone else's home.

This chocolate pie, with its flaky pastry crust and glistening, ruby-colored cranberry topping, is a non-traditional twist on Thanksgiving flavors. With a semisweet chocolate ganache, nutty whole-grain flour in the crust, and tangy fruit, it delivers a novel and enticing new holiday pie.

This pecan tart recipe is the more lavish, decadent cousin of a classic pecan pie. The pecans are enveloped in a rich, chewy caramel filling, and a blanket of velvety smooth chocolate ganache covers the top of the tart, lending it major candy bar vibes with a touch of sophistication.

Shop the recipe: Guittard Semisweet Chocolate Wafers

Based on chess pie, an old Southern favorite, this pie’s texture hits the sweet spot between cheesecake and custard. As it bakes, it also makes its own crackly chocolate-sugar topping, which yields to the dense, fudgy filling beneath.

But worry not: Despite being vegan, it has the fragrant spiced flavor of classic pumpkin pie.

Instead of eggs, this pie relies on cornstarch to bind the gooey filling; coconut cream, meanwhile, stands in for butter. With tons of toasty pecans bound together in a rich, sweet syrup and cradled in a flaky crust, it’s hard to believe this pie is vegan.

#9651. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. #9650. Qu'entraîne réellement le fine-tuning LoRA ?

« LoRA entraîne environ 1 % du modèle » est l'explication habituelle en une ligne. C'est vrai, mais elle cache ce qui décide si un entraînement tient sur votre machine et combien de temps il prend : quelles couches reçoivent des adaptateurs, ce que le rank change au nombre de paramètres, dans quelle précision sont les poids gelés, et combien de pas d'optimiseur un petit dataset donne vraiment.

Voici ces chiffres calculés pour un entraînement concret : Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, rank 16, sur un Mac Apple Silicon de 16 Go. Les réglages sont les valeurs par défaut de l'entraîneur local de l'application de bureau osFoundry, qui est un simple script transformers + PEFT + TRL ; l'arithmétique s'applique donc à n'importe quelle configuration similaire. (La page fine-tuning LoRA de l'appli montre l'interface correspondante.)

Pour une matrice de poids W de forme d_out × d_in, LoRA gèle W et apprend deux matrices, A (r × d_in) et B (d_out × r). La sortie de la couche devient W·x + (α/r)·B·A·x. B démarre à zéro : l'entraînement part donc exactement du modèle de base.

Le nombre de paramètres entraînables de cette couche est r × (d_in + d_out). Il croît linéairement avec le rank et avec la largeur de la couche, pas avec sa surface.

L'entraîneur place des adaptateurs sur les sept projections linéaires de chaque bloc transformer :

Qwen2.5-1.5B a 28 blocs, une taille cachée de 1536, une taille de MLP de 8960 et du grouped-query attention avec 2 têtes KV de 128 dimensions, si bien que k et v projettent vers 256. Par bloc, à r = 16 :

Cela fait 659,456 par bloc, et 18,464,768 sur 28 blocs : 18.5M entraînables sur 1.54B au total, soit 1.2 %.

Deux choses ressortent. Les projections du MLP portent les trois quarts des poids de l'adaptateur ; les omettre (comme le font certaines anciennes recettes, qui n'adaptent que q et v) ramène le total à environ 2.2M, un huitième de la capacité. Et comme le GQA rend k et v étroites, leurs adaptateurs coûtent peu.

Sur le GPU d'Apple, l'entraîneur charge le modèle en float32 :

La demi-précision sur MPS a tendance à produire des pertes NaN, le 32 bits est donc le choix sûr. La base gelée occupe alors 1.54B × 4 octets ≈ 6.2 Go.

La partie entraînable est petite en comparaison. 18.5M de poids en fp32, c'est 74 Mo, les gradients en prennent 74 de plus, et AdamW garde deux estimations de moment par poids, soit encore 148 Mo. Environ 0.3 Go en tout. Le reste du budget part dans les activations, qui dépendent de la taille de batch et de la longueur de séquence (l'entraîneur plafonne les séquences à 2048 tokens ; les réponses courtes de chat en sont très loin).

Avec environ 12 Go sur 16 Go utilisables par le GPU d'un Mac, un modèle de 1.5B en fp32 laisse de la marge. Une base de 7B en fp32 ferait environ 30 Go avant même de commencer l'entraînement. C'est pourquoi, sur un Mac, le modèle de base reste petit, et pourquoi QLoRA (poids gelés en 4 bits) existe ; mais le chemin 4 bits de bitsandbytes exige un GPU NVIDIA, donc sur un Mac c'est du LoRA classique.

L'entraîneur utilise un batch size de 4 avec 4 pas d'accumulation de gradient : chaque mise à jour de l'optimiseur voit 16 exemples. Avec 200 paires :

Trente-neuf mises à jour avec un learning rate de 2e-4 et une décroissance linéaire suffisent à déplacer le ton, pas à enseigner de nouvelles connaissances. C'est ce qu'on constate en pratique : quelques centaines de réponses changent la façon dont un modèle écrit, pas ce qu'il sait.

Après l'entraînement, seul l'adaptateur est enregistré : A et B pour chacune des 196 couches adaptées, quelques dizaines de mégaoctets. Pour l'inférence, l'appli le convertit en fichier LoRA GGUF et llama.cpp l'applique sur une copie quantifiée de la base, ici qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct en Q4_K_M. La base reste partagée : plusieurs adaptateurs (un par ton ou par tâche) coûtent chacun quelques dizaines de Mo.

À noter, l'écart de précision : l'adaptateur a été entraîné sur des poids de base en fp32 et tourne sur des poids en 4 bits. Pour un petit adaptateur de style, la différence passe généralement inaperçue, mais c'est l'une des raisons pour lesquelles un modèle fusionné puis re-quantifié peut se comporter un peu différemment du même adaptateur appliqué à l'exécution.

#9649. Guido van Rossum: The Rise and Fall of Python's Benevolent Dictator

It wasn't the kind of tired a nap fixes. It was the kind that settles into the joints of a sixty-two-year-old man and stays there. Early on the morning of Thursday, July 12, 2018, at his home in Belmont, California, he began to type to the python-committers mailing list, the small closed room where the inner circle of his kingdom did its business.

He was the Benevolent Dictator For Life. The Benevolent Dictator For Life! The title began as a joke, scribbled into the notes of a 1995 meeting in Virginia. Over twenty-three years it hardened into something that was no joke at all. He had the final word on every comma, every keyword, every bit of syntax in a language that had quietly become one of the load-bearing walls of civilization. Python ran Instagram, the recommendation engines at Netflix, the playlists at Spotify. It was the mother tongue of artificial intelligence, of astronomers and geneticists and hedge-fund quants and twelve-year-olds making their first turtle draw a square. And every one of them, in some abstract and terrible sense, answered to him.

No scandal brought him down, no lawsuit, no hostile takeover. Two characters did, a colon and an equals sign:

They called it the walrus. Tilt your head and you see the eyes and the tusks. For months it had been the cause of a civil war: hundreds upon hundreds of emails, a blizzard of Reddit comments, strangers questioning his judgment, his competence, his fitness to rule. The night before, he had formally accepted the proposal, PEP 572. He had won, and winning had cost him so much that he no longer wanted the prize.

Now that PEP 572 is done, I don't ever want to have to fight so hard for a PEP and find that so many people despise my decisions.

Despise. He didn't write disagree with, or question. He wrote despise. That was the word for it.

I would like to remove myself entirely from the decision process.

He was Dutch, and he had never been a man for speeches, least of all dramatic ones. So the message that ended one of the longest reigns in open-source software came out almost offhand. He mentioned "that bus lurking around the corner," the programmer's grim joke about a creator stepping off the wrong curb. He noted that he wasn't getting younger. Then, with that dry deflection of his: (I'll spare you the list of medical issues.)

So what are you all going to do? Create a democracy? Anarchy? A dictatorship? A federation?

And then the last line, the one people would quote for years:

He hit send. The King didn't abdicate in a scene of crashing thunder. He got up from the throne, left the crown on its cushion, and walked out of the room.

How does a holiday hobby, a toy to keep idle hands busy, become a weight that crushes the one who made it? To find out you have to go back to the real cold. Amsterdam, December, 1989.

Picture the city in the last week of the 1980s. The canals have gone black and still, the gables lean over the water like tired old men, and darkness comes down by four in the afternoon. The Berlin Wall fell six weeks ago. History is happening everywhere, and on the eastern side of the city a thirty-three-year-old programmer is bored.

He works at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the CWI, the Dutch national research center for mathematics and computer science. Over the holidays the offices are closed. The young man with the high forehead and the spectacles has a computer at home and, as he'll later put it, not much else on his hands. He also has a grudge that's really more of a grief.

From 1982 to 1986 he had worked on the ABC programming language under Lambert Meertens and Steven Pemberton. ABC was beautiful, an academic's dream of programming for scientists, teachers and beginners, and its most radical idea was significant indentation: the visual shape of the code was its logical shape. No thicket of curly braces and semicolons. You indented, and the indentation meant something.

ABC was also a failure. It was too pure to survive, a sealed world that couldn't talk to the operating system, and the hackers who most needed a clean, high-level tool walked right past it.

By 1989 he had moved on to Amoeba, a distributed operating system project at the CWI, whose team badly needed a scripting language. So, in the dark of that Christmas, he started writing one that would keep ABC's soul but open the windows to Unix and C.

He needed a name. He'd been reading the published scripts of Monty Python's Flying Circus, and he wanted something short, unique, a little irreverent. Python. That was the whole decision, a joke for people who knew the joke.

Stop here a moment, on the young man in the dark, because this is the last moment of perfect innocence in the story. No community, no mailing list, no corporation, no AI, no walrus. One man, a keyboard, a holiday, and the private pleasure of building a thing exactly the way he thinks it ought to be built. He'll spend the next three decades trying to get back to this room.

In February 1991, Python 0.9.0 was posted to alt.sources, one of the dusty Usenet bulletin boards of the early internet. No launch event, no press release. A file appeared, and a few strangers downloaded it.

Hidden inside that file was a wager, the most important bet in the whole story. He'd put it into words years later, in Python's style guide:

Code is read much more often than it is written.

In 1991 the macho culture of programming prized density. Perl hackers wrote one-liners that looked like a cat had walked across the keyboard, and they were proud of it. Cryptic was cool. Unreadable meant you were smart.

Van Rossum bet the other way. If a language made the clear path the easy path, the whole ecosystem would drift toward clarity like water running downhill. And he wrote it into the grammar. In Python, indentation wasn't a suggestion. It was law. Indent wrong and the program wouldn't run. The machine itself would make you write code a human could read.

Years later the core developer Tim Peters boiled the ethos down into nineteen lines of something close to poetry, The Zen of Python, which you can still summon from any interpreter by typing import this. Beautiful is better than ugly. Readability counts. And the line that would come back, nearly three decades later, as a weapon:

There should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it.

Van Rossum didn't write those words. He didn't have to; they described what he'd already built. Python was idiosyncratic, approachable, a little goofy, and because anyone could pick it up and understand it, it spread from hand to hand and machine to machine like a friendly virus.

A crowd gathered around Python, a few dozen people, then hundreds, then thousands, sending bug fixes and feature requests and patches. Somebody had to decide which ones went in. In April 1995, at a meeting of early Python users at CNRI in Virginia, Ken Manheimer's notes named van Rossum "benevolent dictator"; Barry Warsaw is credited with adding "for life." Benevolent Dictator For Life. BDFL.

The joke part was the Benevolent and the For Life. The Dictator part was real. He had the final say on the design of the language. Full stop.

Other open-source founders came to be called BDFLs, but the most famous of them was Linus Torvalds, and the contrast between the two men tells you almost everything.

Torvalds, the creator of Linux, ruled his kernel like a warlord. He swore. He shamed. He sent emails that read like declarations of war, tearing into developers who'd submitted bad code, and he defended his right to do it. Friction forged steel. He liked the fight. (Two months after van Rossum quit, Torvalds would publicly apologize for his behavior and take a break of his own.)

Van Rossum was nothing like that. He came from a country that had pulled itself out of the sea through cooperation. The Dutch call it polderen, after the polders, reclaimed lands kept dry only because farmers and towns and rival interests agreed, painstakingly, on who would maintain which dike. Government by consensus and patient compromise, because if anyone stops pumping, everyone drowns. That was his temperament. He didn't want to yell. He wanted to read the code, weigh the trade-offs, and make people feel heard.

In 1999, working by then at the Corporation for National Research Initiatives in Reston, Virginia, he wrote a funding proposal to DARPA, the Pentagon's research arm, with a title that said everything: Computer Programming for Everybody. Programming as a basic literacy, for high schoolers and hobbyists and ordinary people, not a priesthood. Python would be the vehicle.

It was a generous, democratic vision, and it had a hidden price. If you build a language for everybody, everybody comes. And everybody has opinions.

As Python grew, the process for changing it was formalized as the Python Enhancement Proposal, the PEP. Anyone could write one. Each was argued over in public on the mailing lists. It was open and, on paper, democratic.

In practice it was a funnel. All the anxiety, ambition and ego of tens of thousands of brilliant, stubborn engineers poured down it, and at the narrow end sat one man. He read the threads, hundreds of messages on a single question. He weighed technical merit against aesthetic purity, the beginner against the expert. He was the pressure valve for the whole community, and he wasn't built like Torvalds. He felt it.

This was Google at its most intoxicating, all lava lamps and free lunches, and it ran on his language. Its engineers' motto, made public by the Googler Alex Martelli in 2007, was Python where we can, C++ where we must. Google gave van Rossum half his working time to spend on Python itself. He was no longer a researcher with a hobby. He was a celebrity with a corporate badge, the subject of what one PyCon photographer would caption, without irony, the "obligatory Guido shot."

With the other half he built Mondrian, an internal code review tool named, being who he was, after a Dutch painter. It moved Google's review ritual onto the web, line by line, and taught a generation of engineers his deepest belief: human eyes reading code are the last defense against chaos.

The irony would take years to ripen. He was building a culture of intense, line-by-line, public scrutiny, and that same culture, scaled up past the point where anyone knew each other, would one day be turned on him. On a small team, review is intimate: people who know and trust each other, catching each other's mistakes. Scale it to thousands of strangers on the internet and the intimacy goes sour. It becomes a tribunal.

The first real crack ran right down the middle of the kingdom.

By the mid-2000s, van Rossum could see that some of Python's early decisions, made in a hurry by a young man in a cold winter, were holding the language back. The worst was text. Python 2 muddled human-readable text and raw binary bytes. In 1991 that hadn't mattered. In a global internet of Chinese and Arabic and Hindi and emoji, it was a disaster.

The fix wasn't a patch. It was surgery, and it meant deliberately breaking backward compatibility. Python 3.0 arrived in December 2008, following the blueprint of PEP 3000. It was bold and it was right, and it meant that millions upon millions of lines of Python 2 code wouldn't run on it without being rewritten.

The migration was supposed to be brisk. It took a decade.

It was a grinding war of attrition. Big companies with mountains of technical debt refused to move. Red Hat Enterprise Linux and CentOS 7 clung to Python 2.7 for years. The volunteers who maintained the open-source libraries burned out making their code run on both versions at once. The community split into camps, the Twos and the Threes.

Van Rossum spent those years defending the decision to angry people, playing diplomat between factions of his own. Python 2's death date, first set for 2015, slipped five years to January 1, 2020, with a last-gasp release, 2.7.18, that April.

In the end the transition worked. But victory isn't the same as peace. The schism used up enormous amounts of the Dictator's political capital and stamina. He came out of it weary.

What he didn't know was that the real explosion hadn't even started.

Then, in the 2010s, the ground shifted under the whole of computing. Artificial intelligence and machine learning, which had lived in academic papers for decades, became almost overnight a corporate necessity. The people building them were mathematicians and physicists who thought in matrices and had no patience for Java's ceremony. They wanted a clean, readable wrapper around brutally complicated math.

They chose Python, for exactly the reasons van Rossum had bet on in 1991. NumPy and pandas turned it into a numerical powerhouse, and then it had a gravity of its own: researchers used it, so the tools were built for it, so more researchers came. When Google's TensorFlow and Meta's PyTorch arrived, and later the large language models of OpenAI and everyone else, they all spoke Python.

Look at the size of it! By 2018, nearly 39 percent of developers in Stack Overflow's survey used Python, the fastest-growing major language in the world, and behind them poured biologists, astronomers, accountants and teenagers who had never thought of themselves as programmers at all.

The language had become the scaffolding of the AI revolution and a load-bearing pillar of the global economy. Every machine-learning lab, every startup chasing the next model, every billion-dollar bet on artificial intelligence, bets that by 2026 would swell into the trillions, now ran through a language whose final arbiter was one tired man reading his email. A small tweak under the hood could move a Fortune 500 company's server bills by millions. Every decision landed on him.

He lived it from the inside, too. At Dropbox, which he joined in 2013, he spent years helping migrate more than five million lines of code from Python 2 to Python 3, in the trenches of the very war he had started. Meanwhile the mailing lists filled with a new generation who saw him not as a peer but as a gatekeeper between them and the feature they needed right now. The intimacy was gone. It only needed a spark.

In February 2018 a developer named Chris Angelico, joined by Tim Peters and van Rossum himself, drafted PEP 572: Assignment Expressions.

On paper it was about as dull as language design gets. Python had always kept a strict wall between statements, which do something, like store a value in a variable, and expressions, which evaluate to something. PEP 572 proposed a small door in that wall: a new operator, :=, that would let you assign a value and use it at the same moment, inside an expression. It would save computing expensive things twice and untangle clumsy loops.

Take the old, familiar ritual of reading a file in chunks:

To the purists none of that mattered, because to them PEP 572 was heresy.

They had the scripture to prove it. There should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it. Python already had a way to assign a variable. Now there would be two. To the faithful this was the road to Perl, to show-off one-liners that would baffle beginners. Readability counts! Readability counts! And here was the Dictator himself, they said, selling it out.

What should have been a dry argument about parsing rules turned, almost immediately, into something feral.

The volume of email was staggering. Thread after thread on python-dev and python-ideas, hundreds of messages, every one a little hotter than the last. People dug in. They accused the authors of smuggling C-style syntax into a language that had been designed specifically to reject it. And the poison of modern internet discourse seeped into the technical debate, the way it seeps into everything. People were no longer just disagreeing with the proposal. They were attacking the people: questioning their competence, their motives, their intelligence. And by extension, unavoidably, they were attacking the man at the narrow end of the funnel.

He looked at the evidence, the way he always did. In huge real-world codebases, including Dropbox's, programmers were already doing awkward and risky things to save a line. Used with care, the walrus would make real code cleaner. He believed in it.

On July 9 he announced his intention to accept. On the evening of Wednesday, July 11, 2018, he formally accepted PEP 572 for Python 3.8.

By then the backlash had been building for months, and his decision only fed it. He had ruined the language. People announced they'd ban the walrus from their projects. People talked about forking Python.

This was a man who had spent nearly three decades building a community on collaboration and mutual respect, who came from a culture of the polder and the patient meeting, who had believed that if you made things readable people would understand each other. He was hit with a wave of contempt so large that he couldn't do anything with it. He couldn't answer it or reason with it. It was too much to read and too much to absorb.

Being the final arbiter, the one person who has to soak up the collective fury of thousands of engineers over a colon and an equals sign, had finally changed something between him and the thing he loved. The language that had been his joy had become the source of his misery.

He had won the walrus war and lost the thing he'd been fighting for.

The next morning, roughly fifteen hours after he accepted the proposal, he opened the python-committers list, and you know the rest.

The subject line was almost comically bureaucratic: Transfer of power.

The shock spread across the technology world within hours. Guido steps down. Python's BDFL quits. Reddit threads filled with hundreds of comments. Podcasts rushed out emergency episodes. Developers on the far side of the planet woke to news that felt, absurdly, like the death of a pope, or a parent leaving home.

Look at what he didn't do. He didn't name an heir or hand the crown to a trusted lieutenant. He didn't present a constitution. He did something stranger and, in its way, braver. He threw the question back at them.

Create a democracy? Anarchy? A dictatorship? A federation?

I'll still be here, but I'm trying to let you all figure something out for yourselves.

He would stay on as an ordinary core developer, he wrote. He'd be around to mentor. But the burden of being the last word on everything was over.

The King wasn't overthrown. Nobody stormed the palace. He just stood up, set the crown down on the cushion, and walked out of the room, and behind him the court stood frozen, staring at the empty throne.

What came next was something close to existential dread.

How does a dictatorship invent democracy? How do you decide how to make decisions when your only mechanism for deciding has just walked out the door? The core developers were brilliant engineers, not political philosophers, and they found themselves in a constitutional convention they'd never asked for.

They had good reason to be afraid. Open-source governance is a fragile thing, held together by volunteer labor and goodwill. When a founder leaves, the vacuum is usually filled in one of two ugly ways: a corporation moves in and captures the project, or it shatters into warring forks. The history of free software is littered with the remains of projects that didn't survive their creator's departure.

The models on offer each had a flaw. There was the benevolent dictator, the old Python and the current Linux, where everything hung on one person's health, sanity, and patience, which was exactly the problem they were trying to solve. There was the corporate team, the model of Google's Go, where a company's priorities could always quietly override the community's. There was the meritocratic voting of the Apache projects, which tended to be too heavy, too bureaucratic, too slow for a living language. And there was the elected council, the model of projects like Django, which needed elections, voter lists and rules, and carried the constant risk of gridlock.

Here's the elegant twist. By refusing to name a successor, van Rossum had forced his community to find, in the words of their own scripture, one obvious way, and so they would own it. Seven competing governance proposals were written. In December 2018 the core developers voted, and the winner, by Nathaniel J. Smith and Donald Stufft, became PEP 13, arguably the most important document in Python's history that contains no code at all.

PEP 13 created a five-person Steering Council, elected by the core team after each major release. The authors had studied the failure modes and built in defenses against them. To keep any one company from capturing the language, no more than two council members could work for the same employer; if a third was elected, they were disqualified. Elections used a carefully designed multi-winner voting system meant to produce broad consensus rather than factional victory. And there was a fail-safe, the vote of no confidence: if the council lost the community's trust, the core team could remove a single member or dissolve the whole council and force a new election.

Most telling, the council's mandate was written in van Rossum's image: to seek consensus, to act as a court of final appeal, not a throne, and to use its formal power as little as possible. The Republic would be governed the way the King had always wanted to govern. This time, though, five people would share the weight.

When the first council was elected in early 2019, one of the five names on it was Guido van Rossum. The core developers wanted him there, as a citizen and not a king, and he served one term. Then he stepped back again and left his seat to others.

The real test came with PEP 634: Structural Pattern Matching, a whole new match/case construct for Python 3.10 that took apart complex data structures in a single stroke. It was a far bigger change than the walrus, with far more ways to go wrong.

Again opinion split. Again the threads ran hot. Again people said the language was being ruined.

This time the weight didn't fall on one man. The Steering Council took the pressure and in early 2021 approved the proposal, acknowledging the reservations openly. Nobody burned out. Nobody walked away. The language had survived its creator's leaving, and it was stronger for it.

In October 2019, van Rossum left Dropbox and retired. He was sixty-three. He had seen the Python 3 migration through and laid down the crown. He had earned a quiet life.

Retirement, it turned out, was boring. Then came the pandemic and the empty days of 2020, with nothing to push against. He missed the code. He missed having a team. He missed the satisfaction of a hard technical problem.

In November 2020 he stunned the tech world by coming out of retirement to join Microsoft, in its Developer Division, as a Distinguished Engineer.

Microsoft! The irony was hard to miss. For decades Microsoft had been the great dark empire of the open-source imagination, the company whose leadership had once called Linux a "cancer." Now the creator of one of the most important open-source languages ever was drawing a salary in Redmond. But the Microsoft of Satya Nadella wasn't the Microsoft of the 1990s. It had become, improbably, an open-source powerhouse. And it offered van Rossum something he hadn't really had since that Christmas in 1989: the freedom to just be a programmer.

He put together a small team with the core developer Mark Shannon and went after the oldest complaint about Python: it's slow. No mailing-list wars, no final say, just a hard problem. Their Faster CPython project taught the interpreter to rewrite its own hot code paths as it ran, and Python 3.11, released in 2022, ran about 25 percent faster on average. For a man who had once absorbed a whole community's fury, it was the work he had always wanted: a benchmark, not a referendum.

Corporate patronage cuts both ways, though. In May 2025, in company-wide layoffs, Microsoft ended its support for Faster CPython and let go of Mark Shannon along with fellow core developers Eric Snow and Irit Katriel. The work went on in the open-source community. A year later, in May 2026, van Rossum retired from Microsoft. This time, the language didn't need him to stay.

There was one dragon left, the oldest and biggest: the Global Interpreter Lock, the GIL.

Since its earliest days, CPython had used a single lock that let only one thread run Python code at a time. It kept things simple, and it meant Python couldn't really use the multi-core processors that had become universal. It was a fossil from the young man's cold winter, still lodged in the heart of the machine.

In 2023, the Steering Council took up PEP 703, a proposal by the Meta engineer Sam Gross to make the GIL optional. It was open-heart surgery on the language, with the risk of breaking decades of extensions the whole ecosystem depended on, a far more dangerous change than the walrus.

Think about what that proposal would have done to the old order. If it had landed on the BDFL's desk in 2018, alongside the walrus and on top of everything else, the pressure of managing the fallout might well have broken him outright.

In 2023 there was no single desk to land on. The council accepted PEP 703 as a body and laid out a careful, multi-year road. An experimental free-threaded build appeared in Python 3.13. In Python 3.14, in 2025, it became an officially supported option.

The GIL work belonged to others, to Gross and the council and a long list of contributors, and that was exactly the point. Van Rossum spent those years as an engineer, not a besieged monarch, tuning the interpreter and arguing over implementation details as an equal, while a decision bigger than the walrus was made without him.

He had found his way back to the room in Amsterdam.

In the end, this is a story about the limits of a single human being.

We love the lone genius in technology. We build myths around founders who started in a dorm room or a garage or over a bored Christmas holiday, and we assume the spark of creation comes with the armor needed to rule an empire. We expect the founder to be in command, unbothered, turning any amount of pressure into more power.

But software doesn't have a nervous system. People do.

Python scaled without limit, copying itself across servers and laptops and research clusters until it was the foundation of the AI age. Its creator couldn't scale. There was one of him, with one inbox, one finite supply of patience, and one body that wasn't getting younger. He had built a language on human readability, and it had grown a community that was, in the end, emotionally unreadable.

By walking away, Guido van Rossum won a rare and quiet victory. He escaped the founder's trap, the one that catches creators who can't let go and end up strangling the thing they made, or being strangled by it. He forced his community to grow into a self-governing republic that could carry out pattern matching, a faster interpreter and the slow dismantling of the GIL without tearing itself apart. He made sure Python would outlive him.

The young man in the dark Amsterdam winter of 1989 wanted to build something readable that would let people talk to machines, and to each other, more clearly. He did that. Then it grew into a monster, and the monster nearly ate him. When the fury over a walrus pushed him to the edge, he walked away from his crown, and in doing so he saved his kingdom. More importantly, he saved himself.

Guido van Rossum was tired. Then, at last, he rested. And then, because he'd always been a programmer before he was a king, he went back to writing code, until in 2026, at seventy, he retired once more. This time he went on his own terms.

Author's note: This profile is narrative nonfiction. Interior moments and scene-setting are imagined, drawn from the public record. Quotations from the "Transfer of power" email are from van Rossum's message to the python-committers list on July 12, 2018.

The Ghost of Columbia Still Haunts Starship's Heat Shield

#9648. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

"IT added me to the share group. I still get Access Denied."

Permissions look right in AD or Entra. The share ACL looks right. The user is sure they're in the group. And yet… Access Denied. 😤

Usually nothing is "wrong" with the permissions. The PC is still holding yesterday's security token.

Don't trust the portal alone. Check what this Windows session thinks:

Windows builds your access token at logon. That token carries your group SIDs. Locking the screen keeps the same token. So:

For Entra-joined devices, a full sign-out/sign-in is what refreshes the modern auth token too. A quick lock/unlock won't cut it. 💡

If it's a classic SMB/file share and they're still blocked after a fresh logon:

Then reconnect to the share (open \\fileserver\share again). Kerberos will request a new service ticket with the updated groups.

Prefer PowerShell for the reconnect check?

If port 445 fails, you're in DNS/VPN/firewall territory — not permissions.

At the help desk, "permissions are fine" often means "the directory is fine." The endpoint is still running on an old token. Teaching users (and yourself) to verify membership → full sign-out → purge tickets closes the ticket without a pointless ACL rewrite. 💪

#9645. Binance's Post-Mortem Is Out. The $6.3 Billion Hack Started With a Job Offer.

In September, a software engineer at Binance got a message on a legitimate job-hunting site. The sender called himself a project director. The engineer's profile mentioned his work at Binance.

Round one was a live video interview with an "HR representative," who shared a social media account full of personal photos and videos to build trust. Round two happened in a popular chat app, with a man claiming to be the CEO of a company that didn't exist. Near the end, he asked the engineer to download a short coding assignment.

Within weeks, about $6.3 billion left Binance's hot wallets in the largest crypto theft on record.

Last week I wrote about how Binance lost that money without losing a single private key. At the time, Binance had only said the trouble "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop." On Tuesday, 3 November, it published its post-mortem. The laptop turns out to be the last chapter of a story that started in June.

It opens with a line you rarely see from a crypto exchange: "This should not have happened."

It began with a search engine. A wallet DevOps engineer (the report calls him Engineer A) searched for a popular AI coding tool and installed it through what turned out to be a tampered Homebrew installation. Binance files it under supply-chain attack.

Binance's security team caught it. They flagged the anomaly, replaced his device and rotated his credentials, which is exactly what a good team should do.

It was still too late in one respect. The attacker now knew who Engineer A was, what he worked on, and who sat next to him on the wallet infrastructure team. The malware was gone; the map of people stayed.

That map explains why Engineer B got such a friendly message in September. Binance calls the approach more deceptive than any social engineering it had seen before. It also had plenty of company: the exchange says it detected and blocked 57 suspected state-sponsored attack attempts in 2026 alone, using fake job interviews, booby-trapped developer tools, poisoned browser extensions and fake video-call apps.

"We've identified dozens of other job interview compromises that have led to wallet compromises."

Tom McLouth, senior intelligence analyst at Chainalysis, speaking to The Hacker News

The "assignment" ran malicious code during setup. It deleted the real copy of pyenv, a common tool for managing Python versions, from the engineer's Homebrew folder, slipped a doctored copy into its place, and opened a line to a server the attacker controlled. According to the report, the malware was a zero-day, endpoint security didn't catch it at the time, and it scrubbed its own traces.

One laptop, one trusting moment, and the attacker had a foothold.

For weeks, nothing visible happened. Then, on 20 October, the attacker used Engineer B's machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of two more engineers' computers, Engineer A's and Engineer C's.

On Engineer A's machine they found the prize: a token with permission to deploy containers.

Binance hasn't explained how its own AI tool let an outsider jump from one computer to another. That gap matters. Companies are rolling out internal AI assistants with wide access to code, tickets and machines, and this may be the first billion-dollar case of one being turned into a lateral-movement tool.

Between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC, the attacker logged onto Engineer C's computer, used Engineer A's stolen credentials, deployed a container and ran a malicious script. That gave them Binance's internal wallet-signing service, the system that authorizes transactions.

Nine minutes later, at 20:05 UTC, five Binance hot wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233.46 million XRP to the attacker. Solana, Optimism, Bitcoin and Ethereum followed.

This is the part that should worry every custody engineer.

Binance suspended withdrawals that night. Money kept leaving anyway. The attacker had used the signing service to approve 50 EIP-7702 authorizations, which gave an attacker-controlled contract execution rights over a hot wallet. Those rights lived on-chain. Binance's withdrawal switch had no say over them.

To cancel a delegation, the wallet has to sign a revocation. Binance's hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which splits signing power across several parties so that no single stolen key can move funds. That same design meant no single key could cancel the delegation quickly either. Binance had to build a special revocation procedure on the spot.

The last unauthorized transfer, 2,961.9 ETH, finalized at 23:56 UTC; it had been broadcast earlier and sat pending. At 00:10 UTC on 30 October, Binance signed a new authorization that pointed the wallet's delegation at the zero address, which finally cleared it, just over four hours after the first coins moved.

The control built to stop theft slowed the cleanup. I don't think that argues against MPC. It argues for rehearsing the emergency path (revoke, rotate, freeze) before you ever need it.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system in a new environment, rebuilt the internal AI tool and its access controls, replaced devices, decommissioned the affected engineers' credentials and tokens, scanned every employee device, and tightened wallet-service risk controls. It's also bringing in independent security firms and setting up a research fund on AI security in blockchain systems. About $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted, and 98% of affected tokens were replenished by 31 October.

"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done."

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng, speaking to CNBC

Binance calls this an initial report and says some measures will stay private so attackers can't plan around them. Fair enough. Still, three questions are open: how the internal AI tool was abused, which AI coding product was impersonated in June, and why a container-deployment token was sitting on an engineer's laptop at all. Those are the answers other exchanges need most.

The uncomfortable lesson is that the attacker spent months on people and only hours on systems. Engineer A did nothing reckless; he searched for a tool his whole industry uses. Engineer B did what thousands of developers do every week when they look for a new job.

"It should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, quoted by Help Net Security

So if you work anywhere near production, never open an interview assignment on a work machine. Use a throwaway virtual machine or a separate personal device, every time.

And if you run a security team, put "our engineers are job hunting" on your threat model. At Binance, that line was worth $6.3 billion.

This follows my earlier piece, Binance Lost $6.3 Billion to Its Own Signing Machine. Details come from Binance's post-mortem of 3 November 2026 and the reporting linked above.

Disclosure: I hold no position in Binance and have no affiliation with the company.

#9644. LLM Security Needs Capability Scoping, Not Better Prompts

TL;DR — Filtering and classifier-based guardrails treat prompt injection as a text-matching problem, but attackers only need one novel phrasing to win. The durable fix borrows from network security's 'assume breach' posture: tag content by provenance, propagate that taint through the pipeline, and scope what tools an agent can invoke based on where its instructions actually came from. Defense in depth here means the model can be compromised and the system still doesn't act.

Every team building LLM agents eventually ships the same first line of defense: a classifier or a system prompt rule that tries to spot malicious instructions before they reach the model. Every team building LLM agents also eventually watches that defense fail. Not because the classifier was badly built, but because it was solving the wrong problem. Prompt injection isn't a text-matching problem. It's a trust-boundary problem, and you cannot patch a trust-boundary problem with better pattern recognition.

Input filtering assumes malicious intent has a detectable signature. It doesn't, because the "attack" is just natural language doing what natural language does: persuading. A filter trained on "ignore previous instructions" gets bypassed by a document that frames the same request as a customer support ticket, a translation task, or a nested quotation. The attacker's search space is the entire space of human rhetoric. Your defense's search space is whatever patterns you've seen in red-team logs. That's not a fair fight, and it never converges.

This is the same lesson network security learned decades ago with signature-based antivirus. Signatures catch yesterday's malware. They never catch a competent adversary who can test against your detector before shipping. The industry's answer wasn't better signatures — it was to stop assuming the perimeter holds and start designing systems that stay safe even when it doesn't. LLM security needs the same pivot. Stop trying to keep bad instructions out of the context window. Start designing so that instructions arriving from the wrong place simply cannot do anything dangerous.

Here's the structural mistake most agent architectures make: by the time text reaches the model's context window, its origin has been flattened. The system prompt, the user's message, a retrieved document, a tool's JSON response, and a scraped web page all become the same undifferentiated token stream. The model has no architectural reason to treat a sentence buried in a PDF differently from a sentence its operator wrote on purpose. Of course it can be talked into treating the PDF's sentence as an instruction — nothing in the representation tells it not to.

The fix is to stop discarding provenance at ingestion and instead carry it as metadata through the entire pipeline, the way a compiler carries taint annotations through a data-flow graph. Every unit of content entering the context gets tagged with where it came from: operator-authored, authenticated user, retrieved document, third-party API response, untrusted web content. That tag isn't decoration — it has to survive concatenation, summarization, and chunking, and it has to be inspectable at the point where the system decides to act. This is more engineering than prompting. It means your retrieval layer, your tool outputs, and your context assembler all need to emit and preserve provenance, not just text.

Provenance only pays off if something downstream uses it to make a decision. That something is the tool-calling layer, and this is where defense in depth has to live, because it's the only place where language turns into consequence. A model hallucinating a wrong answer is embarrassing. A model invoking send_email or execute_transfer because a calendar invite told it to is a breach.

The pattern to copy here is capability-based security, the same principle behind OAuth scopes and least-privilege IAM roles. An agent shouldn't have blanket access to every tool it knows about; it should hold capability tokens scoped to the current task, and — critically — those tokens should be gated by provenance. A request to transfer funds or modify a production record should require that the instruction originated from an authenticated, high-trust channel, not from text that arrived via a retrieved document or a tool response. If the triggering instruction's provenance tag says "untrusted web content," the tool-calling layer refuses, full stop, regardless of how convincingly the model argues for it.

This reframes the model's role. The model proposes actions. It does not get to be the sole authority deciding whether an action executes. That authority sits in a layer that can be audited, tested, and reasoned about independently of the model's weights — which matters, because you cannot formally verify what a transformer will output, but you absolutely can formally verify what a policy engine will authorize.

It's worth being precise about scope, because conflating jailbreaks with injection leads teams to build the wrong defense. A jailbreak targets the model's own alignment — getting it to say something it was trained not to say. Prompt injection targets the application built around the model — getting it to act on attacker-supplied instructions it was never meant to obey. Capability scoping and provenance tagging don't make the model immune to jailbreaks; they make jailbreaks less consequential, because even a model that's been talked into agreeing with an attacker still has to pass its proposed action through an authorization layer that doesn't care how persuasive the conversation was. A compromised model proposing an unauthorized wire transfer is a non-event if the tool layer requires a trust tag the injected text can't produce. That's the entire point of defense in depth: no single layer has to be perfect, because each layer's failure is contained by the next one.

Teams often interpret "defense in depth" as stacking more filters: an input classifier, then a guardrail model, then an output scanner. That's depth in name only — it's the same category of defense repeated three times, and a single clever prompt can slip through all three if they share the same blind spot. Real depth means layers that fail differently. A provenance tag doesn't care about phrasing, so it's not fooled by the rhetorical tricks that fool a classifier. A capability scope doesn't care what the model said, so it's not fooled by a jailbreak that bypasses the guardrail model. Each layer should be defeated by a fundamentally different kind of attack, which is exactly what makes it expensive for an adversary to chain a bypass across all of them.

This costs real engineering effort: instrumenting your retrieval and tool pipelines to carry metadata, building an authorization layer that's independent of the model, and accepting that some legitimate-looking requests will get blocked because their provenance doesn't clear the bar. That friction is the price of containment. The alternative — hoping your filter has seen every phrasing an attacker might try — isn't a security posture. It's a bet you will eventually lose, and in an agentic system, losing means a tool call executed with real-world consequences, not just an awkward chat response.
